papers.title: Folk Theorems for Social Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25280v1

summary.one_liner: We study repeated games with purely informational externalities.

papers.abstract: We study repeated games with purely informational externalities. Each player observes a single conditionally independent signal and then repeatedly takes publicly observed actions to maximize their expected discounted payoff, which depends only on the state and their own action. We show that, when there are sufficiently many players and they are sufficiently patient, there exist equilibria where information is aggregated: the players' payoffs approximate the full-information payoff. This holds even if actions are uninformative under myopic play. Conversely, even if myopic play reveals the state, there also exist equilibria where information is not aggregated: payoffs approximate those under autarky. Our results speak to the range of possible outcomes of social learning games with forward-looking agents.

papers.title: A Simple Proof of Koray's Theorem
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25748v1

summary.one_liner: In this note, I provide a direct and self-contained proof of Koray's (2000) theorem, by which a neutral and unanimous social choice function is universally self-selective if and only if it is dictatorial.

papers.abstract: In this note, I provide a direct and self-contained proof of Koray's (2000) theorem, by which a neutral and unanimous social choice function is universally self-selective if and only if it is dictatorial. Koray's (2000) original proof relies on results by Sen (1970) and Houthakker (1950) to construct a social welfare function for each alternative set. He then shows that these functions are Paretian and independent of irrelevant alternatives, allowing him to apply Arrow's (1950, 1951) impossibility theorem. Instead, I construct a cyclic preference profile and show that the voter who ranks the chosen alternative first is the dictator on every finite nonempty alternative set.

papers.title: Uniqueness, Proximity, and Scaling in Atomic Splittable Polymatroid Congestion Games
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25757v1

summary.one_liner: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational player-specific affine latencies with positive slopes.

papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational player-specific affine latencies with positive slopes. The algorithm first computes equilibria of associated integer-splittable games, in which demands are allocated in multiples of a common packet size. For arbitrary polymatroid bases, no polynomial-time algorithm for these discrete equilibria was previously known. We provide such an algorithm and use progressively finer packets to recover the continuous equilibrium exactly. Our proof uses the multiple-exchange theorem of Oki and Schwarcz (2025) to obtain two exchange matchings that yield equilibrium proximity under changes of packet sizes and ranks, independently of cost coefficients. We then bound the matching deficiency caused by rank changes and construct compatible submodular rank roundings. Together these give a polynomial-time packet-halving algorithm using polynomially many submodular-function minimizations and exact rational arithmetic. The analysis rests on a uniqueness theorem of independent interest: for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks and continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, convex latencies, we prove uniqueness of equilibria, resolving a previously open problem.
